**June 23, 1956 — A Saturday**

You arrived on a Saturday in early summer, in a year so crowded with world-altering events that historians return to it repeatedly. Nineteen fifty-six was not a quiet year. It was a year of eruptions — political, cultural, geological — and you were born right in the middle of it, in the weeks before several of them came to a head.

---

**On the exact day you were born, Egypt held a referendum.**

Gamal Abdel Nasser ran as the sole candidate for President of Egypt on June 23, 1956, in a plebiscite that confirmed him with near-unanimous approval and ratified a new Egyptian constitution. The vote was a formality, but the moment was not. Nasser was consolidating one of the most consequential political transformations in the postwar Middle East — the end of Egypt's subordination to British imperial influence, and the emergence of pan-Arab nationalism as a defining force. Exactly one month and three days later, on July 26, 1956, Nasser would nationalize the Suez Canal, triggering a crisis that ended Britain and France's pretensions to global imperial power and reshaped the entire Cold War map. The referendum on your birthday was the formal prelude to that upheaval.

---

**One week after your birth, America built itself a new skeleton.**

On June 29, 1956 — six days after you were born — President Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act, authorizing the Interstate Highway System. Forty-one thousand miles of controlled-access highways would be built across the country over the following decades, funded by the federal government. The United States that you grew up in — its suburbs, its motels, its truck stops, its road trips, its commuter culture — was physically shaped by a law passed the week you entered the world. The country was literally being redesigned as you drew your first breaths.

---

**A bus was still refusing to move in Montgomery.**

When you were born, the Montgomery Bus Boycott was in its seventh month. Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat in December 1955. The Black community of Montgomery, Alabama, had been walking to work ever since — carpooling, enduring harassment, sustaining a disciplined act of collective resistance that lasted 381 days total. Martin Luther King Jr., then 27 years old, was its young and newly prominent spokesman. The boycott would end in December 1956 with a Supreme Court ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. You were born in the middle of one of the founding acts of the American civil rights movement.

---

**Children your age were the first generation safe from polio.**

Jonas Salk's vaccine had been licensed in April 1955, and by the summer of 1956, mass vaccination campaigns were well underway. For every generation of parents before yours, summer had carried a specific dread: the swimming pools that closed, the iron lungs in hospital wards, the inexplicable paralysis that could strike any child. Your parents had grown up with that fear. You did not. The polio vaccine was one of the great public health achievements of the 20th century, and children born in your cohort were among the first to benefit from it as an ordinary fact of childhood rather than a miraculous relief.

---

**Elvis Presley was 21 years old.**

In early 1956, "Heartbreak Hotel" reached number one. By the time you were born in June, Elvis had already appeared on The Milton Berle Show and caused a national uproar with his dancing. He was filming his first movie. Teenagers were screaming in ways that alarmed their parents. Something was breaking open in American culture — a generational assertion, a new relationship between youth and sound and the body — and it was happening in the weeks around your birth. You would grow up entirely inside the world rock and roll made.

---

**The Cold War was thawing, carefully, dangerously.**

In February 1956, Nikita Khrushchev had delivered his "Secret Speech" to the Communist Party congress, denouncing Stalin's crimes. The news leaked. The communist world trembled. In Hungary, reformers were emboldened — and in October 1956, four months after your birth, Soviet tanks would crush the Hungarian Revolution in what became one of the defining atrocities of the Cold War. The thaw Khrushchev had offered turned out to have hard limits. You were born in the brief moment between the speech and the crackdown, when the limits were not yet fully visible.

---

**The arc of a lifetime**

You are 70 now.

You were seven when Kennedy was shot in Dallas. Old enough to remember the television coverage, the riderless horse, the world going briefly silent. You were twelve in 1968 — that extraordinary year when King was killed in April, Robert Kennedy in June, and the Democratic convention erupted in violence in August. You were thirteen when Apollo 11 landed on the moon. Eighteen during Watergate's final unraveling.

The personal computer appeared when you were in your twenties. The internet rewired daily life in your late thirties and forties. A smartphone arrived in your pocket and rendered obsolete nearly every specialized device you had ever owned. You were 45 on September 11, 2001.

The Soviet Union that shadowed your entire childhood ceased to exist when you were 35. The British Empire that Nasser was defying on the day you were born is now fully historical. The highways signed into law the week after your birth are showing their age.

---

**What kind of world**

The summer of 1956 was a pivot. Empire was ending, visibly. A new global order — shaped by the Cold War, by American economic dominance, by television and automobiles and nuclear weapons — was settling into place. The people around your cradle had survived the Depression and the war and were now, tentatively, beginning to believe in prosperity.

You grew up in the world that pivot made, and lived long enough to watch that world transform again, completely, into something none of those people around your cradle could have imagined.

Seventy years is a long measurement of change.
